en: The Buddha spoke this *Dharmādharma-sūtra*, which is found in the *Madhyama Āgama*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. This...
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus replied,
“So be it,” and listened to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"There are dharmas of the noble ones that a bhikṣu should listen to; there are also dharmas of those who are not noble, which he should listen to, listen to thoroughly, become well-acquainted with, and reflect upon thoroughly."
“Yes, Bhiksus,” they replied, and having received the instruction from the Buddha, the Buddha then spoke thus:
“What is the conduct that is not the dharma of a worthy one?

If a bhikṣu comes from a great clan and delights in the Path, desiring to train in the Path, yet there are other fellow-studying bhikṣus who do not come from a great clan, that bhikṣu—on account of his being from a great clan—becomes conceited about himself and deceives others; this is the conduct that is not the dharma of a worthy one.”
“What, then, are the qualities of a noble person?
A noble person trains with this resolve: ‘I need not belong to a great clan; I am able to abandon lust, I am able to abandon hatred, and I am able to abandon delusion.’”

Furthermore, there may be a monk who does not come from a family of great renown, yet possesses the skillful means to receive the Dharma; he teaches the Dharma as it is, practices according to its essentials, and acts in accordance with the Dharma for the sake of its reputation.
He practices the Dharma as it is and realizes the truth of the Dharma, neither praising himself nor deceiving others—this is the dharma of the noble ones.

"Sometimes a certain bhikṣu is exceptionally handsome in appearance, while other bhikṣus are not; because of this physical beauty, he praises himself and disparages others. This is not the dharma of a worthy one."

The wise person is not like this; the wise person reflects for themselves: "Though my physical form may be handsome, I shall certainly not rely on this [beauty] to be able to sever lust, to be able to sever hatred, and to be able to sever delusion."

At times, there may be a bhikṣu who is not handsome, yet merely according to the extent of the Dharma he receives and practices, he gains praise and a good reputation; he receives the Dharma with truthfulness and acts in accordance with the Dharma, neither praising himself nor deceiving others—this is the quality of a worthy one.

"Sometimes one bhikṣu is skilled in speech and eloquent, while other bhikṣus are not; he then praises himself and disparages others on account of his skill in speech and eloquence. This is not the dharma of a noble one."

The wise person is not like that; the wise person trains with the thought: "I shall not necessarily follow merely because it is well-spoken, nor follow merely because it is known to be well-spoken, but rather that which can sever sensual desire, sever ill will, and sever delusion."

“Furthermore, there may be a monk whose speech is neither skillful nor beautiful, and who does not speak well; yet, having received the teaching in accordance with the Dharma, he practices it to some extent, and thereby gains respect and a good reputation. This dharma arises from receiving the teaching and practicing it with truthfulness; he neither praises himself nor deceives others—this is the dharma of the noble one.”

“Furthermore, there may be a certain bhikṣu who is senior in years, possesses great renown, and is well-known for his abundant wealth; whereas other bhikṣus are not like him, he then relies on his seniority, his great renown, and his wealth to praise himself, become arrogant, and deceive others. This is not the Dharma of a worthy one.”

"The wise person is not like that; the wise person simply reflects and trains with this resolve: 'I shall certainly not [attain my goal] because of being advanced in years, nor because of having many acquaintances, nor because of having acquired much merit; rather, it is through the ability to sever greed, the ability to sever hatred, and the ability to sever delusion.'"

"Or there may be a bhikṣu who is neither advanced in years, nor possesses many acquaintances, nor has abundant merit; yet, by merely receiving the Dharma, desiring to follow the Dharma, and practicing the Dharma to some extent, he thereby gains renown."
To follow the Dharma in accordance with the Truth, neither praising oneself nor being arrogant, and not deceiving others—this is the dharma of a noble person.

However, at times, there may be a certain bhikṣu who, having heard the teachings, knows how to recite the sūtras, knows the Vinaya, and possesses mastery of the scriptures; yet, because other bhikṣus do not possess such mastery, he praises himself, becomes arrogant, and deceives others based on that mastery and proficiency. This is not the dharma of a noble person.

“The wise one is not like that; the wise one merely reflects: ‘I must study this so that, even if I do not enter [the stream], nor through mastery of the scriptures, I may be able to sever greed, sever hatred, and sever delusion.’”

"Suppose there is a bhikṣu who has not entered [the stages], nor is he versed in the sūtras, but merely receives the Dharma and practices in accordance with the Dharma; seeking only to practice in accordance with the Dharma, he thereby gains respect and a good reputation."
This is the noble dharma: from upholding the Dharma and practicing in accordance with the Dharma, one does not praise oneself, does not become arrogant, and does not deceive others.

"At times, a certain bhikṣu seeks for himself and does not seek through the acquaintance of others; he does not go beyond seven houses, sits in one place, eats at one time, and does not take more after that. If other bhikṣus do not act as he does, he then praises himself, becomes arrogant, and deceives others by saying, 'I eat only one meal and do not take more after that. This is not the dharma of the noble ones."

The wise person is not like that; the wise person simply trains, thinking: "I need not necessarily follow [the rule] of not taking food after one meal. It is for this reason that they are able to abandon greed, able to abandon hatred, and able to abandon delusion.

At times, a bhikṣu may observe the practice of eating only once a day and not taking food after [the mealtime], but rather receiving the Dharma, following the Dharma, and correctly receiving in accordance with the Dharma; through this he gains respect, and through this he gains renown.
This is the truth of the Dharma that accords with the Dharma: it is the way of the noble ones, wherein one does not praise oneself, does not become arrogant, and does not deceive others.

"Suppose there is a certain bhikṣu who dwells among the mounds in a cemetery; because he possesses only three robes by name, other bhikṣus do not equal him. Yet, on account of that name alone, he praises himself, becomes arrogant, and deceives others. This is not the dharma of a worthy one."

“The wise person is not like that; the wise person simply considers: ‘By training myself, I shall certainly be able—regardless of whether I am known by three names—to abandon greed, to abandon hatred, and to abandon delusion.’”

Furthermore, there may be a bhikṣu who does not possess the three robes by name, yet he receives the Dharma and practices in accordance with the Dharma, correctly receiving and following the Dharma; because of this, he gains respect and a good reputation.
This practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma is true; he does not praise himself, he is not arrogant, nor does he deceive others—this is the dharma of the worthy one.

"Sometimes a certain bhikṣu dwells in the open air, sometimes under a tree, and sometimes in an empty marsh or among graves; regarding his bedding and requisites, he thinks other bhikṣus are not as good as he is. Because of this, he praises himself, becomes arrogant, and deceives others. This is not the Dharma of a worthy one."

"The wise person is not like that; the wise person simply considers: 'By training myself, I shall certainly not [rely] on this exposure, this tree-shade, or this empty marsh to be able to sever greed, to sever hatred, and to sever delusion.'"

"Or at times, a bhikkhu may not possess the aforementioned qualities, yet he receives the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma and correctly practices in accordance with the Dhamma; through this, he gains honor and a good reputation.
This practice of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma is true, and it is the way of the noble ones: to not praise oneself, to not be arrogant, and to not deceive others."

"Suppose a bhikṣu has attained the first dhyāna while other bhikṣus have not; because of this attainment of the first dhyāna, he praises himself, becomes arrogant, and deceives others. This is not the way of a worthy person."

"The wise one is not like that; the wise one merely trains in the first dhyāna. The Buddha has said that when one knows for oneself, 'I have attained this Dharma and realized its truth,' yet does not praise oneself, does not become arrogant, and does not deceive others—this is the way of the wise one."

"Furthermore, there may be a bhikkhu who possesses the qualities of the second dhyāna, or the qualities of the third dhyāna, or the qualities of the fourth dhyāna, as was explained regarding the first dhyāna; this is the noble one's Dhamma."

"Suppose at times a bhikṣu understands the practice of emptiness, or at times understands the practice of consciousness, or at times understands the practice of impermanence, or at times understands the practice of being without thought while practicing with thought; yet other bhikṣus do not equal him. Consequently, he develops the practice of having thought or being without thought, and then praises himself, becomes arrogant, and deceives others. This is not the way of a worthy one."

The wise person is not like that; the wise person simply considers that there is no perception and no mental formations of perception. The Buddha has said that from the reckoning "I am this," there arises the acceptance of phenomena and conformity with the truth of phenomena. To not praise oneself, not be arrogant, and not deceive others—this is the dharma of the wise person.
The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus!

I have already taught the dharmas of the noble ones, and I have also taught the dharmas of those who are not noble. Bhikṣus, you should reflect for yourselves; you should also reflect upon the dharmas of the noble ones."
Having reflected upon what is not the Dharma of the wise, one should practice the Dharma of the wise, abandon the Dharma of the unwise, and undertake the Dharma of the wise.
A monk who follows the Dharma should train himself in this way.
When the Buddha had spoken this, the bhikṣus received it with a mind of focused application.
This is the Sūtra on Dharma and Non-Dharma spoken by the Buddha.
